captions.instagram:
How does a bicycle work?

Two triangles, a chain and a wheel of thin wires, and a machine that balances itself. Take a bicycle apart in 3D and ride its physics.

→ A bicycle is two triangles, two wheels, a chain and a way to steer.
→ Triangles can’t change shape, so thin tubes make a light, stiff frame.
→ Gears trade effort for speed: a smaller rear cog turns the wheel more per pedal stroke.
→ On a hill, part of gravity pulls you back. A bigger rear cog shrinks the push you need.
→ Too slow, and a bicycle wobbles and falls over.

Play with it yourself. It's free and open source: glassbox-production-fd52.up.railway.app/cycleclear (link in bio)

youtubeLong.title: How does a bicycle work? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
Two triangles, a chain and a wheel of thin wires, and a machine that balances itself. Take a bicycle apart in 3D and ride its physics.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox-production-fd52.up.railway.app/e/cycleclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/cycleclear

In this video:
• A frame of two triangles. Most bikes use a diamond frame: two triangles sharing the seat tube.
• A chain links pedals to wheel. Your feet turn the cranks and the front chainring.
• Gears trade effort for speed. The gear ratio is front teeth divided by rear teeth.
• A moving bike balances itself. When a moving bike leans, its front wheel steers into the lean, bringing the wheels back under it.
• Wheels hang on tensioned spokes. Every spoke is pulled tight to about 1,000 newtons.
• Brakes turn motion into heat. Stopping means getting rid of kinetic energy, which grows with the square of speed.

Glassbox opens one box a day: an interactive model of how something works, plus the code behind it.
